# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Definition and Epidemiology

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a form of pregnancy-associated heart failure that affects previously healthy women. PPCM is a form of systolic heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction affecting childbearing women during pregnancy or in the early postpartum period, and delays in diagnosis may occur because the symptoms and signs of PPCM can mimic the normal findings of late pregnancy and the peripartum period. The first formal case definition emerged from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute workshop in 2000, requiring heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, and absence of pre-existing structural heart disease [1]. PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion in women presenting with heart failure and systolic dysfunction; the 2010 ESC Working Group definition includes development of heart failure toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, and left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction generally below 45 percent—a definition since expanded to include the last trimester and the first 6 months postpartum. [2,3]

The incidence varies markedly by geography and ethnicity. In Durban, South Africa, a PPCM prevalence of 1:1000 live births was reported, while an earlier Johannesburg study described a rate of 1:3000. [4] In the United States, PPCM occurs in approximately 1:2000 deliveries. [5] A nationwide US analysis examined temporal trends in incidence and outcomes, querying the 2004–2011 Nationwide Inpatient Sample to identify women with PPCM, because the reported incidence in the US varies widely and limited information on trends was available. [6]

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is multifactorial, with two converging mechanisms dominating contemporary understanding. The prolactin hypothesis emerged from murine work showing that female mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of stat3 develop PPCM, with enhanced cardiac cathepsin D expression generating a cleaved antiangiogenic and proapoptotic 16 kDa form of prolactin. [7] Understanding has highlighted oxidative-stress-mediated cleavage of prolactin into a toxic 16-kDa fragment that induces detrimental but potentially reversible effects on heart function. [8] A complementary "vascular" hypothesis proposes that PPCM is associated with systemic angiogenic imbalance, accentuated by pre-eclampsia; mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α develop profound PPCM, which is entirely rescued by pro-angiogenic therapies. [9] In humans, the late-gestation placenta secretes VEGF inhibitors such as soluble FLT1, accentuated by multiple gestation and pre-eclampsia, and the resulting anti-angiogenic state correlates with subclinical cardiac dysfunction. [9] These mechanisms have been synthesized in successive position statements [2,10,11] and reviews [12,13].

## Genetics

A genetic predisposition overlapping with dilated cardiomyopathy is now well established. In 172 women with PPCM, sequencing of 43 dilated-cardiomyopathy-associated genes identified 26 distinct rare truncating variants in eight genes, with a prevalence (15%) significantly higher than in a reference population. [14] Two-thirds of truncating variants were in TTN, almost all located in the titin A-band, and their presence correlated with lower ejection fraction at 1-year follow-up. [14] A subsequent multicenter study confirmed and extended these findings on the genetic landscape of PPCM [15], underscoring shared mechanisms with familial cardiomyopathies [16].

## Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis, and Outcomes

Prospective cohorts have clarified outcomes. The IPAC study prospectively evaluated recovery of left ventricular ejection fraction and clinical outcomes, enrolling and following 100 women with PPCM through 1 year postpartum, with echocardiography at baseline and at 2, 6, and 12 months. [17] Most women recovered, but 13% had major events or persistent severe cardiomyopathy; Black women had more dysfunction at presentation and follow-up, and severe baseline dysfunction and greater remodeling predicted less recovery. [17] The global ESC EORP registry described clinical presentation, management, and 6-month outcomes in women with PPCM across 49 countries. [18] Just under half of women experienced myocardial recovery within 6 months, and neonatal death occurred in 5%. [18] Earlier registry data characterized the worldwide clinical phenotype [19], and inflammatory and immune mechanisms have been a recurrent focus of study design and analysis [20].

## Management

Standard heart failure therapy—adapted for pregnancy and lactation—forms the backbone of management, as detailed in ESC position statements [10,11] and pregnancy guidelines [21]. Disease-specific therapy targeting prolactin has been most investigated. A proof-of-concept trial found that prolactin, mainly its 16-kDa form, is a key factor in PPCM pathophysiology, and blockade with bromocriptine—shown to prevent disease onset in mice and high-risk women—was tested by randomizing 20 women with acute severe PPCM to standard care or standard care plus bromocriptine. [22] A subsequent multicenter trial compared dosing regimens: considering an anti-angiogenic cleaved prolactin fragment causal for PPCM, 63 patients with ejection fraction ≤35% were randomized to short-term or long-term bromocriptine in addition to standard heart failure therapy. [23] These trials build on foundational mechanistic [7] and observational [24,25] work, and the bromocriptine concept has been reviewed extensively [26,27,28]. Registry analyses continue to refine its role in routine practice [29], and the relationship between breastfeeding, immune activation, and recovery remains an area of active investigation [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is an increasingly understood but still challenging cause of maternal morbidity and mortality. Convergent hormonal-vascular mechanisms, a genetic predisposition shared with dilated cardiomyopathy, and prospective registries have transformed the field, while prolactin-targeted therapy exemplifies bench-to-bedside translation. Early recognition, guideline-based heart failure management, and multidisciplinary care remain central to improving outcomes.
